title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6779 – Reuters estimate
body: The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through October, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.--- The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.Summary: The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets.

title: US Natgas Prices Edge Higher
body: US natural gas prices inched up to $2.97 per MMBtu on Wednesday, attempting to recover from a four-week low seen in the prior session, as stronger LNG export activity and lower production partially offset soft demand amid mild weather conditions. title: Japan Trade Gap Widens Sharply
body: Japan's trade deficit widened sharply to JPY 536.6 billion in September 2026, up from JPY 277.7 billion a year earlier, surpassing market expectations of a JPY 181.0 billion shortfall and marking the fifth consecutive monthly deficit. title: Macro pulse: Is the BOJ about to raise interest rates at the worst possible time?
body: I don't think anyone would want to the be in the BOJ's shoes right now. On the one hand, inflation pressures are giving policymakers every reason to keep raising interest rates. But on the other hand, Japan's economy is already dealing with expensive energy imports and a weak yen - not to mention a very uncertain global outlook. If that isn't problematic enough, then here's the kicker. The inflation pressures that are building aren't exactly the kind that the BOJ has been hoping for. The central bank has spent decades in trying to nurture a healthier cycle of rising wages, stronger consumer spending, and sustainable price increases. For the most part, those efforts went nowhere. And it took a global economic reset from the Covid pandemic to finally give Japan a get-out-of-jail-free card. Remember, Japan spent much of the last thirty years struggling with stagnant wages and prices. Businesses were reluctant to raise prices, workers weren't getting any meaningful wage increases, and consumers had grown accustomed to things staying relatively cheap. Then came the Covid pandemic, followed by global supply chain disruptions and a surge in commodity prices. Suddenly, businesses had little choice but to raise prices as inflation started making its way back into the Japanese economy. Initially, that was largely cost-push inflation too.

title: Why Treasury yields move together but become more volatile further out the curve
body: Treasury yields are primarily driven by expectations for the future path of Federal Reserve monetary policy. This relationship is especially strong at the front end of the yield curve, where yields are closely linked to expectations about how the Fed will adjust interest rates over the near-term. However, monetary policy expectations remain important even at the long end of the curve. The difference is that longer-term yields are also more sensitive to changes in the economic outlook, inflation expectations and the compensation investors demand for holding long-duration bonds, called term premium. The front-end is driven by monetary policy expectations The 2-year Treasury yield is one of the most useful indicators of market expectations for Federal Reserve policy. If markets begin to expect the Fed to raise interest rates in the coming months, the two-year yield will generally rise. Conversely, if economic data weakens or inflation moderates, markets will start to price in rate cuts and the 2-year yield will generally fall. The key point is that markets are forward-looking. Treasury yields reflect expectations for future short-term interest rates over the life of the bond. Consequently, yields will move well before the Fed actually changes its policy rate. That doesn't mean the market will always be right. Sometimes the market gets things wrong, but the change in expectations still drives yields higher or lower depending on the economic context and incoming information.

title: Social unrest pressures European markets

The problem is that France's budget deficit reached 5.1% of GDP in 2025, while public debt approached 120%, leaving the government with little room to support households. Actually, it is now pushing for €54 billion in spending cuts in its 2027 budget, as the fiscal outlook could otherwise deteriorate further, but getting them through amid social unrest won't be easy. Demonstrations also took place in Liège, Belgium, in early October before spreading to other cities across Wallonia and Brussels, as well as Ireland, Spain, Italy, Germany, Greece, and Austria. While largely peaceful, the unrest is putting pressure on European bond markets and the EUR/USD currency pair. In France, for example, long-term government bond yields have reached 5.5%, surpassing US yields for the first time since 2013. The cost of insuring against a French default has also climbed to its highest level since 2013. European equities are also under pressure, with rising energy prices amid the war in the Middle East, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, and concerns over returns on AI investments adding to the strain and further weighing on sentiment.
